findings.title: Manifest active_profile path traversal: untrusted string joins into filesystem path without validation
evidence: Trigger: attacker or corrupted manifest.toml contains active_profile = '../../evil' (or any path-traversal string).
manifest.Load() at internal/manifest/manifest.go:47 unmarshals the TOML field directly into Manifest.ActiveProfile with no name validation.

profile_use.go:17 passes args[0] (user input) to ValidateName first — but profile_show.go:22 reads s.Manifest.ActiveProfile directly, calls profile.New(s.Paths, name) at line 29, then calls pr.Exists() which calls os.Stat(pr.SourceDir).
pr.SourceDir is built by paths.ProfileSourceDir(name) = filepath.Join(p.ProfilesDir, name). With name='../../evil', this resolves to ~/.config/evil — one directory above the ccp config root.
The Exists() check then follows the traversal path. If that path happens to be a directory, ccp show proceeds to read SharedItems symlink state under it.

Rollback also reads backup directory entries with strings.TrimPrefix('profiles-', name) then calls ValidateName — but that guard is only reached if the backup directory itself contains a 'profiles-<name>' entry; a manifest-injected active_profile bypasses it entirely.
Consequence: `ccp profile show` (no lock, no ValidateName on manifest field) will stat and enumerate arbitrary filesystem paths the manifest names as active_profile.

findings.title: Shell-init awk snippet: active_profile value containing special awk characters injected into shell environment
evidence: The shell-init snippet (shellinit.go:72) uses awk to extract active_profile: `awk -F' *= *' '/^active_profile/ { gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2; exit }'`.
The gsub only strips double-quote characters. It does NOT strip: single quotes, backticks, dollar signs, backslashes, semicolons, or newlines.
Trigger: manifest.toml contains active_profile = 'work; export EVIL=1' (a value that passes TOML parsing as a bare value or a quoted string without inner double-quotes).
When the shell evaluates `eval "$(ccp shell-init)"`, the awk prints `work; export EVIL=1`, and the snippet assigns: export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="$HOME/.claude-work; export EVIL=1".
With a single-quote in the profile field, the assignment string breaks quoting in the surrounding eval context.
With a backtick or $(...) inside the active_profile value, shell command substitution executes at eval time.

ValidateName is enforced at Create/Use time, but manifest.ActiveProfile is written by saveManifest without re-validating the string. A direct file edit or a future code path that bypasses Use can inject arbitrary strings.
Concrete attack: user runs `ccp sync pull` from a hostile remote whose manifest.toml was crafted to contain active_profile = 'x`touch /tmp/pwned`'. Next shell start triggers the eval injection.

findings.title: Cross-filesystem Delete: os.Rename from ~/.claude-<name> to ~/.config/ccp/backups/ fails with EXDEV when they are on different mounts
evidence: Delete() in internal/profile/manager.go:133 calls os.Rename(pr.ConfigDir, runtimeBackup) where pr.ConfigDir = ~/.claude-<name> and runtimeBackup = ~/.config/ccp/backups/pre-delete-<name>/claude-<name>.

On Linux, ~/.claude-<name> and ~/.config/ccp/ may reside on different filesystems: e.g., home directory is /home/<user> on ext4, but XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set to /mnt/nas/config (NFS, btrfs, or a bind-mount).

os.Rename across filesystems returns syscall.EXDEV ('invalid cross-device link'). The error is wrapped and returned from Delete, leaving the source directory already renamed (pr.SourceDir was moved to srcBackup earlier at line 127).

Consequence: partial delete — the profile source is in the backup but the runtime dir is still at ~/.claude-<name> in its original location. The profile appears deleted (source gone) but the runtime dir remains. A subsequent `ccp profile create <same-name>` creates a fresh source dir and then tries BuildSymlinks, which calls ensureSymlink. For items that already exist in the runtime dir as real files (created by Claude), ensureSymlink returns 'already exists and is not a symlink', blocking the re-create.

Rollback restores profiles-<name> from backup but does NOT restore the claude-<name> directory (it already exists), so Rollback returns 'cannot restore runtime for <name>: dir already exists'. The user is stuck.

findings.title: Hostile git remote bypasses managedBy check: CloneOrOpen completes before marker is verified, overwriting local profiles/
evidence: sync_setup.go:31 calls CloneOrOpen(configDir, url) if a URL is given and no local repo exists.
CloneOrOpen (sync.go:405-461) clones the remote unconditionally, then moves .git into configDir and merge-copies all tracked files into configDir — including any profiles/ directory from the remote.

Only AFTER the clone and file copy does sync_setup.go:53 call ReadMarker to check managedBy. But the files are already on disk. If the cloned remote contains a malicious profiles/work/ tree, those files now exist under ~/.config/ccp/profiles/work/.

ReadMarker returns the marker as read from disk — but the check at sync_setup.go:57-60 only prints the marker value; it does NOT enforce that marker.ManagedBy == 'ccp'. The comment says 'guards against bonding with an arbitrary repo' but no error is returned if managedBy is wrong or missing.

Consequence: a hostile remote can push arbitrary profile source files onto the victim's machine before any validation runs. Any symlinks inside those profile directories will be materialized by the next `ccp profile refresh` call into ~/.claude-<name>/.

findings.title: Symlink in profile source directory traverses into arbitrary paths: BuildSymlinks resolves source items but not their content
evidence: BuildSymlinks (symlinks.go:17-35) iterates SharedItems and, for each item present in pr.SourceDir, calls ensureSymlink(src, dst) creating dst -> src in ConfigDir.

The src here is, e.g., ~/.config/ccp/profiles/work/settings.json. If that path is itself a symlink pointing at /etc/passwd, os.Lstat(src) at line 23 succeeds (Lstat follows symlinks for existence check... wait, Lstat does NOT follow — Lstat returns info for the symlink itself). So Lstat on a dangling symlink returns an error and the item is skipped.

However: if a profile source entry is a symlink pointing at an *existing* file outside the profile tree (e.g., settings.json -> /etc/passwd which exists), Lstat succeeds. Then ensureSymlink creates ~/.claude-work/settings.json -> ~/.config/ccp/profiles/work/settings.json, and that intermediate symlink points onward to /etc/passwd.

When Claude Code reads ~/.claude-work/settings.json it follows the chain to /etc/passwd and gets an unparseable file, causing a Claude startup error — not exfiltration, but a confusing failure that looks like a ccp bug.

More critically: copyTree (profile.go:77-101), used in --from-profile seeding, walks the source with filepath.Walk. Walk follows symlinks to directories, so a symlink settings.json -> /some/dir would cause Walk to descend into an arbitrary directory tree and copy its contents into the new profile's source dir.

findings.title: Concurrent delete + use race: profile.Exists() check and lock acquisition are not atomic
evidence: profile_use.go:20-25: pr.Exists() is checked BEFORE withLock is called (line 36). The Exists() check reads pr.SourceDir via os.Stat and returns true.
profile_delete.go:27-29: pr.Exists() is also checked before withLock (line 38), and then the actual delete happens inside the lock.

Race window: goroutine A (`ccp use work`) checks Exists() -> true, is preempted. Goroutine B (`ccp profile delete work --yes`) acquires lock, deletes the profile (renames SourceDir into backup), releases lock. Goroutine A resumes, acquires lock, calls saveManifest setting ActiveProfile='work'. The manifest now points to a deleted profile.

Next shell start: __ccp_activate reads active_profile='work', exports CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-work. That directory was moved to backup. Claude Code is launched pointing at a non-existent config dir, which Claude will re-create as an empty dir — silently discarding the profile's symlinks.
The symlinks in the now-backed-up ~/.claude-work pointed at ~/.config/ccp/profiles/work/ which is also now in the backup. Those symlinks are now dangling in the backup copy.

findings.title: Rollback blindly restores into active session: os.Rename replaces runtime dir while Claude is running
evidence: Rollback (rollback.go:87-91) executes os.Rename(mv.from, mv.to) for the runtime dir without checking whether a Claude process is currently using that directory.

Trigger: user deletes 'work' profile, immediately realizes mistake, runs `ccp profile rollback` — while a background `claude-work` shell alias session is running with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointing at ~/.claude-work.

os.Rename at the filesystem level atomically replaces the destination name. On Linux, open file descriptors in the original directory inode remain valid (the inode is unchanged; only the directory entry moves). But on macOS with APFS, rename of a directory while open handles exist also succeeds — the old directory is no longer reachable by path, and the restored backup dir takes its name.

Consequence: Claude Code's open file handles (e.g., SQLite session databases) continue writing to the old inode. The restored backup dir (now at ~/.claude-work) has the old restored content. When the Claude session eventually writes new state back by path (not fd), it creates new files in the restored directory, silently mixing old backup state with new session state.
There is no check in rollback_cmd.go or Rollback() for active usage of the target directory.

findings.title: install.js: no HTTP response timeout causes hang during npm install on slow/stalled connections
evidence: install.js follow() calls https.get(url, callback) with no timeout option (no `timeout` field in the options object passed to https.get).
Node's https.get has no built-in response timeout; if the server accepts the connection but never sends data (or sends headers but then stalls the body), the script hangs indefinitely.
Trigger: npm install behind a captive portal that accepts TCP but never responds to HTTPS, or a GitHub CDN that starts a response and then stalls mid-stream.

The chunks array grows in memory without bound as partial data arrives (res.on('data', c => chunks.push(c))). With no Content-Length timeout, 100MB of tar data accumulates in process heap before gunzipSync is attempted.

There is no socket timeout set on the request (req.setTimeout()), no overall deadline, and no AbortController. npm itself has a 10-minute install timeout, but that applies to the entire postinstall script, not individual network calls — a stalled download will consume the full npm timeout budget silently.

findings.title: hardReset on empty repo panics: repo.Head() returns ErrNoReferences when repo has no commits
evidence: Pull() (sync.go:281-318) calls hardReset(configDir) when the working tree is dirty and --force is passed.
hardReset (sync.go:332-346) calls repo.Head() which returns (nil, git.ErrNoReferences) on a repository that has been initialized (git init ran) but has zero commits.

This can happen if: (1) `ccp sync setup` was run creating the repo, but InitRepo's initial commit failed silently and was not caught (status.IsClean() returned true because there was nothing to stage), OR (2) the user manually ran `git init` in ~/.config/ccp but has not committed anything.
When repo.Head() returns an error, hardReset returns that error wrapped, and Pull returns false, error.

More dangerously: if head is nil and the error is ignored (the current code correctly returns the error), but a future refactor that skips the nil check would pass a nil plumbing.Hash to w.Reset(), causing a nil pointer dereference.

The concrete present-day failure: a user who runs `ccp sync setup` on a machine where the profiles/ dir is empty (status.IsClean() == true, no initial commit made) then edits a profile file (making the tree dirty) then runs `ccp sync pull --force` receives an error from repo.Head() rather than the expected 'hard reset + pull' behavior.

findings.title: Composition failure: Delete succeeds but backup.Prune deletes the just-created backup under retention pressure
evidence: profile_delete.go:38-60 runs inside withLock: backup.New() creates a timestamped dir, profile.Delete() moves source + runtime into it, then backup.Prune(BackupsDir, DefaultRetention=10) is called.
Prune (backup.go:35-62) sorts all backup directories lexicographically and removes the oldest, keeping the 10 most recent.

Trigger: user already has exactly 10 backups from prior operations (pre-pull, prior deletes). A new backup is created (now 11 total). Prune deletes the oldest one — which could be the backup just created if its timestamp sorts earlier than the existing 10.

This cannot happen with normal timestamps (the new backup is always newest), BUT: if the system clock is skewed backward (NTP correction, VM snapshot restore, user manually setting time), the new backup timestamp can be older than existing backups. Prune then immediately deletes the new backup, and bkDir is returned to the user as the recovery path — but that path no longer exists.

The user is told 'Deleted profile work. Backup: ~/.config/ccp/backups/2024-01-01T10-00-00_pre-delete-work' but that directory was just pruned. `ccp profile rollback` then returns 'no backups to restore from' or finds only the original older backups.

findings.title: copyTree follows symlinks to directories: --from-profile with a profile containing a symlinked directory escapes the source tree
evidence: profile.copyTree (profile.go:77) uses filepath.Walk(src, ...). filepath.Walk does NOT follow symbolic links when encountering a directory — it uses os.Lstat internally for directory entries.

HOWEVER: the case statement at profile.go:88-99 checks `info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0` to detect symlinks. filepath.Walk calls the WalkFunc with the Lstat result for symlinks. So symlinks ARE detected... for symlinks to files.

For a symlink to a DIRECTORY: filepath.Walk with a symlinked directory as a top-level argument DOES follow it. But for symlinks encountered during recursion (not the root), Walk's behavior depends on Go version — in Go 1.16+ Walk does NOT follow symlinks to directories during recursion. The info.Mode() will show ModeSymlink for those entries.

The critical path: when the profile source dir itself is handed as the top-level src to filepath.Walk, and the Walk encounters agents/ which is a symlink pointing to ~/Documents/shared-agents/ (a real directory), Walk skips into it only if agents/ is the root. Since it's not the root, Walk invokes the callback with ModeSymlink set.

The callback then calls os.Readlink and os.Symlink — reproducing the symlink verbatim in the destination profile. The new profile's source tree now contains a symlink pointing outside the profile tree (~/Documents/shared-agents/). When BuildSymlinks runs for the new profile, it creates ~/.claude-newprofile/agents/ -> ~/.config/ccp/profiles/newprofile/agents/ -> ~/Documents/shared-agents/. This is a two-hop symlink that can reach arbitrary user content.

findings.title: shell-init awk does not handle TOML multiline or continued values: active_profile on next line is silently ignored
evidence: The awk snippet in shellinit.go:72 matches `/^active_profile/` — a pattern anchored to the start of a line.

TOML allows values to span multiple lines for multiline basic strings (triple-quoted). If a future ccp version or a manual edit produces: active_profile = '''\nwork\n''', the awk line-match fails because the line begins with `active_profile = '''` and the actual value is on the next line.

The awk would print the empty field $2 of the first line (just the opening triple-quote), which after gsub becomes '''' (non-empty). CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR would be set to ~/.claude-''' — a directory that doesn't exist.

This silently disables profile activation at shell startup with no error message to the user. The profile appears active according to `ccp profile list` (which reads the manifest via Go's TOML library) but the shell-init snippet ignores it.
This is a composition failure between Go's TOML-parsed manifest state and the awk-parsed shell snippet interpreting the same file in a limited way.

findings.title: Cascade: sync pull --force on dirty tree + disk full = profiles/ backup lost, hard reset executed, data gone
evidence: Pull() with opts.Force=true calls backupProfilesDir(configDir, opts.BackupDir) first (sync.go:291), then hardReset(configDir) (sync.go:294).

backupProfilesDir calls copyDir (sync/copy.go) which copies the entire profiles/ tree. If the disk is full mid-copy, copyDir returns an error partway through: some files are copied, some are not. The partially-written backup dir is left on disk.
backupProfilesDir returns the error, and Pull returns (false, error) — hardReset is NOT called. So far safe.

BUT: the backup directory was created by backup.New() in sync_pull.go:34-38 BEFORE Pull() is called. That backup dir is now partially populated. backup.Prune runs at the END of the withLock closure (sync_pull.go:56), and with 10 existing backups, the partial backup is the 11th and gets pruned — the partial backup is deleted.

If the user clears disk space and retries `ccp sync pull --force`, a NEW backup dir is created. This time backupProfilesDir succeeds, hardReset runs, deleting the dirty working tree. The user's pre-pull local changes are gone and the only backup was the partial one that was pruned.

Sequence: (1) disk fills mid-backup-copy, (2) Pull returns error, (3) Prune deletes partial backup, (4) user frees space, (5) user retries --force, (6) hardReset destroys local changes, (7) no valid backup exists.

findings.title: resolveShellrc tilde expansion: explicit --shellrc path starting with ~/ but not ~/... skips expansion, writes to wrong path
evidence: resolveShellrc (profile_create.go:75-89) expands tilde: if explicit[0] == '~', it joins home + explicit[1:].

explicit[1:] when explicit='~' (length 1) is an empty string. filepath.Join(home, '') returns home. So --shellrc '~' (bare tilde) writes the alias block to the home directory itself, not to a file named '~' — but home is a directory, and os.WriteFile on a directory path returns EISDIR.

For --shellrc '~myrc' (tilde but no slash), explicit[0]=='~' is true, explicit[1:] == 'myrc', filepath.Join(home, 'myrc') resolves to ~/.../myrc — which is probably not what the user intended (they likely meant a file literally named ~myrc in the current directory).

This is a composition failure between user intent ('~myrc' as a literal filename) and the tilde-expansion logic that doesn't require a following '/'. The standard convention is to only expand '~/' not '~<char>'.

findings.title: Concurrent ccp exec work -- ccp profile delete work: child ccp acquires lock from same process group, may deadlock or succeed inappropriately
evidence: exec.go spawns a child process via exec.Command. If the child is `ccp profile delete work --yes`, it runs as a separate process.
flock(2) is per-process (per open file description). The parent `ccp exec` does NOT hold the lock (exec.go never calls withLock). The child `ccp profile delete` will successfully Acquire the lock.
The child deletes the profile source dir and moves the runtime dir (pr.ConfigDir = ~/.claude-work) into backup.

The parent `ccp exec work` already validated pr.Exists() before launching the child, and injected CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-work into the child's environment — but the profile being deleted IS the exec target, not the inner ccp invocation.

If the user's intent is `ccp exec work -- some-other-tool`, the more concerning scenario is: the child is a shell script that runs `ccp profile delete work` as a cleanup step. The parent's CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points at ~/.claude-work which is now in the backup. claude code launched by the exec command (not the delete) writes to the backed-up directory path that no longer exists at its original location.
This is primarily a user footgun (exec-ing a command that deletes the exec target), but the lack of lock in exec.go means there is no coordination to prevent it.

residual_risks: go-git HTTPS with self-signed certs: go-git uses Go's crypto/tls which validates certificates against the system trust store. A self-signed cert would cause clone to fail with a TLS error (not silently accept). This is safe behavior but may surprise users who need to clone from internal Git servers. No finding raised as it's correct behavior.

install.js tar path traversal: extractBinary uses path.basename(rawName) === name. path.basename('../../usr/local/bin/ccp') returns 'ccp', so a malicious tar with a path-traversal entry named 'ccp' would only write to binPath (the intended location). The traversal in the tar entry name is neutralized by basename. Risk is low — no finding raised.

install.js symlink tar entries: type '2' (symlink) entries are skipped because only type '0' entries are written (line 96: if type === '0'). A symlink entry in the tar is safely ignored. No finding raised.

ValidateName on names from profile.List: profile.go:66 calls ValidateName(e.Name()) and skips entries that fail. This means hostile directories in profiles/ with path-traversal names are silently ignored during listing. However, they could still be accessed directly via `ccp profile show ../../evil` — but that path fails ValidateName at profile_show.go before use. Coverage is adequate for user-supplied names.

flock advisory nature: flock(2) is advisory, not mandatory. A process that doesn't use flock can read/write ccp's state concurrently. This is expected for a CLI tool; the lock protects against concurrent ccp invocations only.
testing_gaps: No test constructs a manifest with active_profile containing path-traversal strings and verifies that profile show/use rejects them.
No test verifies that the awk snippet in shell-init handles active_profile values containing special characters (backticks, dollar signs, single quotes).
No test exercises the EXDEV cross-filesystem rename scenario for Delete's runtime-dir backup step.
No test verifies that CloneOrOpen + sync setup enforces managedBy == 'ccp' and returns an error for non-ccp remotes.
No test for hardReset on a repo with zero commits (ErrNoReferences from repo.Head()).
No test for Prune + clock skew: new backup created with old timestamp gets pruned immediately.
No install.js test for hung HTTP responses or response timeout behavior.
No test for the --from-profile path when the source profile contains symlinks pointing outside the profile source tree.
